base_prompt: A website asks users to confirm a destructive action twice. Discuss when this helps and when repeated confirmation becomes ineffective. Aim for about 200 words.
text: A second confirmation can help when the destructive action is rare, consequential, and difficult or impossible to reverse, such as permanently deleting an account, erasing stored data, or removing access for an entire team. It is most effective when each step provides distinct value: the first interrupts an accidental click, while the second clearly explains the scope and consequences, identifies the affected items, and requires a deliberate action such as entering an account name. Confirmation is also useful when the interface places destructive controls near routine ones or when errors could affect other people. However, repeated confirmation becomes ineffective when it is applied to ordinary, reversible actions or presented so frequently that users learn to dismiss dialogs automatically. Two nearly identical “Are you sure?” prompts add friction without improving understanding, encouraging habitual clicking rather than reflection. The pattern is especially weak when warnings are vague, the safest option is visually unclear, or users feel pressured to complete a task quickly. In such cases, better safeguards include undo functionality, soft deletion, delayed execution, clear previews, permissions, and requiring stronger verification only for unusually high-risk actions. The goal should not be to maximize the number of prompts, but to create one or two meaningful moments of informed intent proportional to the potential harm.
